messages.body_plain:
Dear list,

I ran a line transect analysis with only a single transect (k = 1)
and now I am trying to understand how Distance computes degrees of
freedom in this case.
As far as I understood
1) Since empirical estimation is not possible Distance automatically
assumes a Poisson distribution for n, i.e. var(n) is computed as n
(or overdisp * n if an overdispersion factor has been specified)
2) Since degrees of freedom for the encounter rate are zero (df(n/L)
= 0) confidence intervalls of n/L are based upon quantiles of the
normal distributon instead of the t-distribution.
3) The degrees of freedom of the object or school density (Ds) is set
equal to the degrees of freedom of f(0), i.e. df(Ds) = df[f(0)]

What I can not reconstruct is how Distance computes the degrees of
freedom for the density of individuals (D). In general this is done
by the Satterthwaite approximation described on page 78 in the 2001
Distance book, but this does not work here since df(n/L)=0.

So the question is: Are the three statements above correct an how
does Distance compute df(D) when df(n/L) = 0?

Thanks and best regards

	Felix

messages.body_plain:
Dear List,

I=92m trying to get density estimates for several forest bird species usi=
ng=20
Point transect sampling and I have some questions that I wanted to post=20=

here.

Problem 1: Unbalanced survey effort
I work in several plots and data were gathered monthly during different=20=

years (2 seasons/year). My problem is that survey effort (the number of=20=

visits to each point) varies between months and geographical plots (due t=
o=20
bad weather, some plots could not be visited in some months). Does this=20=

mean I cannot pool data from all months together? The thing is that I=20
haven=92t enough data to analyze per month, and I hoped I could work per=20=

season or per year.=20
What I could do is to look for the plot and season with the lowest survey=
=20
effort and randomly pick data from the others to make survey effort equal=
,=20
but this would mean that I loose many data. Is there a possibility to=20
solve this problem in a different way?

Problem 2: Poststratification or stratification?
Behalf of the fact that stratification is recommended for geographical=20=

data, whereas poststratification is recommended for non-geographical=20
variables, what is the consequence of using poststratification instead of=
=20
stratification? When I run my analysis, stratification by stratum (plot)=20=

doesn=92t work, whereas poststratification does work. I wonder why, and w=
hat=20
would be the consequence in using poststratification here.

Problem 3: Relationship between cluster size and density=20
Has anyone experienced a significant negative relationship between cluste=
r=20
size and radial distance yet? What could be the biological explanation fo=
r=20
this? Should I estimate cluster size using the size-bias regression=20
method? To me, it seems as if the relation, though significant, is not=20=

biologically relevant. Clusters of more than one individual were rarely=20=

observed and the fact that those clusters were observed at rather short=20=

distances from the observer doesn=92t need to be a consequence of it (sin=
ce=20
a correlation doesn=92t describe causality). Therefore, I thought of=20
calculating mean cluster size using the mean size of observed clusters,=20=

although I don=92t feel fully comfortable with that.

I hope somebody can help me out with these problems!
Thanks in advance,

Val=E9rie

If all you need is an overall density or abundance estimate, you could=20
put points with the same (or similar) number of visits into a stratum,=20
then conduct a stratified analysis.  You could also do this initially to=20
see if there are differences in these strata with respect to animal=20
density.  If the estimates don't differ signifcantly, it might be=20
reasonable to assume that number of visits is uncorrelated with density,=20
in which case you could pool data from repeat visits, ignoring the=20
variation in effort.

> > Problem 2: Poststratification or stratification?
> > Behalf of the fact that stratification is recommended for geographical=20

> > data, whereas poststratification is recommended for non-geographical=20

> > variables, what is the consequence of using poststratification instead =
of=20
> > stratification? When I run my analysis, stratification by stratum (plot=
)=20

 what=20

> > would be the consequence in using poststratification here.

> >  =20
In what sense does stratification not work?  Choosing an option where=20
you stratify for encounter rate and assume a common detection function=20
across strata (or if this is unreasonable, a common model for the det=20
fn, but using the multiple covariate distance sampling engine of=20
Distance to allow for differences in detectability between plots) should=20
be OK.

> > Problem 3: Relationship between cluster size and density=20

> > Has anyone experienced a significant negative relationship between clus=
ter=20
> > size and radial distance yet? What could be the biological explanation =
for=20

> > this? Should I estimate cluster size using the size-bias regression=20
> > method? To me, it seems as if the relation, though significant, is not=20

> > biologically relevant. Clusters of more than one individual were rarely=

> > observed and the fact that those clusters were observed at rather short=

ince=20

> > calculating mean cluster size using the mean size of observed clusters,=

> > although I don=92t feel fully comfortable with that.

This is common, and generally arises because cluster size is=20
underestimated at larger distances.  The regression method then corrects=20
for this underestimation (provided you get good cluster size estimates=20
for clusters close to the point), so use the regression method still.

We put the numbers of each record in a cluster i.e. the individuals recorded at a distance of 300 m were summed into one record and the cluster was given the summed number. The data was separated into two strata (forest edge and forest core); the area of these strata, the line transects, the line lengths, the clusters and the four separate animal classes were included and the project was created. Then an analysis was run (CDS, no stratification, all key functions and AIC were used)

However, the output shows much fewer animals than the expected (from rough estimations)....

Can anyone help???

messages.subject: Transect sampling of sheep on mountainous Cyprus (was "Help.....")
messages.subject_clean: Transect sampling of sheep on mountainous Cyprus (was "Help.....")
messages.body_plain:
Dear CK and Distance list:

Let me address each of your issues in succession.

If you have placed your transects in the valleys of the mountain range
(because it is easier to navigate in the valleys than the hillsides),
then you have not randomly sampled the landscape.  This will interfere
with your ability to make inferences from your sample.  It would be
better (and more taxing) to place your transects randomly.  Consult
section 7.2.1 of Buckland et al. (2001) regarding transect layout.

For the extent of visibility of 400-500m, this is known as the
truncation distance (denoted by the symbol 'w').  If you enter each of
your detections separately, Distance 5.0 will examine those
perpendicular distances, and determine your truncation distance to be
the maximum distance at which a detection was made.  You can also alter
this truncation distance, w, to make it smaller as is customary in many
analyses.

I believe you are using the term 'cluster' in a manner different from
which we are accustomed.  We refer to a cluster as a group of individual
animals that are detected at the same time.  I believe your use of the
term is what Buckland et al. (2001) describe as 'grouped data.'  This is
where you combine detections over distance categories for subsequent
fitting of the detection function.  It is best practice to enter your
detections into Distance as ungrouped; i.e., enter each of your
detections as separate records.  If it is necessary to convert data to
grouped, this can simply be done using Distance.  See section 1.5 of
Buckland et al. (2001).  It may be the case that several sets of
cutpoints might be employed during the exploratory phase of your
analysis, so allowing Distance to make these conversions rather than
having to re-enter data for each cutpoint analysis is much easier on
your fingers.

I understand your use of the vegetation to create strata, but it is not
clear how you used the animal age and sex classes in your analysis.  You
could enter them into your Distance project as fields in the observation
layer, and apply the data filter to select each age class for analysis
and estimation.

Those are my immediate thoughts.  I don't know if that helps explain the
results you obtained.

         I N T E R N A T I O N A L   S T A T I S T I C A L
                E C O L O G Y   C O N F E R E N C E
____________________________________________________________________

             University of St Andrews, 9-11 July 2008

We would like to announce an international conference on all aspects of
statistical ecology, to be held in St Andrews, Scotland.  More details
are on our conference website:

http://www.creem.st-and.ac.uk/isec2008

Invited speakers are Ken Burnham, Anne Chao, James Clark, Jim Nichols,
Shirley Pledger, Roger Pradel and Carl Schwarz.

We will soon issue an invitation to submit abstracts.  While papers on
any topic in statistical ecology will be welcome, we especially invite
papers on:  mark-recapture methods;  distance sampling methods;  other
abundance estimation techniques;  monitoring of biodiversity;  survey
design and analysis for estimating population trends;  modelling of
spatial trends in animal density;  integrated population modelling;
stochastic population dynamics modelling;  stochastic multispecies
modelling;  stochastic modelling of animal movement.

The conference is being organised by the UK National Centre for
Statistical Ecology.  Enquiries and expressions of interest can be
submitted to:

isec...@mcs.st-and.ac.uk <mailto:isec...@mcs.st-and.ac.uk>
